• This paper develops a variational data assimilation (DA) method and applies it
to a simple solar wind propagation model.
• Such a DA scheme enables the inner boundary of the solar wind model to be
updated using observations in near-Earth space.
• Experiments performed with both synthetic and STEREO observations show

I didn't find a 2023 paper by Milosic on EUHFORIA background solar wind validation for 2019–2020. The closest match is a 2019 Solar Physics paper by Hinterreiter et al., which may be what the query is pointing to.

- **Paper:** "Assessing the Performance of EUHFORIA Modeling the Background Solar Wind," published in Solar Physics, vol. 294, article 170, in December 2019 (DOI 10.1007/s11207-019-1558-8). The arXiv version is 1907.07461. Published: 2019-12-05.
- **Method:** The authors ran the basic EUHFORIA 1.0.4 setup with default inputs, modeled background solar wind without CMEs, and compared the results against ACE in-situ data.
- **Scope:** The study is the first performance assessment of EUHFORIA's solar wind modeling and flags limitations of its default setup. It is not a 2019–2020 validation, and I found no Milosic author on it.
- **Related work:** A 2018 conference poster by Hinterreiter covered an earlier validation at low (2008) and high (2012) solar activity. A later BELSPO project summary reports that the solar wind speed is underestimated and density overestimated on average, and that results depend strongly on EUHFORIA's simple coronal model.

The arXiv preprint is **arXiv:2109.07873** by Evangelia Samara and co-authors, first submitted 16 September 2021 and revised in February 2022. It proposes dynamic time warping as a way to validate modeled solar wind time series, and tests it on WIND observations and EUHFORIA output at L1. The method warps sequences in time to align them at minimum cost, using dynamic programming.

The paper describes two uses. One produces a sequence similarity factor that scores a forecast against ideal and non-ideal reference predictions. The other measures the time and amplitude offsets between the best-matched points in the two series. The authors position the method as a middle ground between correlation coefficients and point-by-point comparison. They report that it can evaluate both fast and slow solar wind.

I could not confirm from these results that the arXiv version is the 2022 Space Weather publication, so that link needs checking against the journal page. A related 2021 EGU abstract (EGU21-12459) by the same group describes the same DTW approach applied to EUHFORIA datasets. Two later papers also use DTW to assess EUHFORIA: an ApJ (2024) study that evaluates predictions at Earth from PSP-calibrated WSA boundary conditions, and an NSF-indexed study that uses EUHFORIA-driven OpenGGCM output to predict Dst.

The search found the paper's draft manuscript and several secondary sources describing it.

- **The paper:** A January 2015 draft of "On the Role Played by Magnetic Expansion Factor in the Prediction of Solar Wind Speed" lists Pete Riley and Jon A. Linker (Predictive Science) and C. Nick Arge (AFRL) as authors. The draft was submitted to the Journal of Geophysical Research, with a DOI of 10.1029/ left blank. I did not find the final published version or its exact citation details in these results, so check the journal listing before citing it.
- **Main finding, per secondary sources:** Wikipedia's summary of the Wang–Sheeley–Arge model reports that Riley and colleagues concluded the expansion factor plays "only an indirect role" in determining the speed at 1 AU, while the distance to the coronal-hole boundary correlates more directly with observed speed. An Eos article on the work says the authors suggest that models have evolved so much that the expansion factor underlying the 25-year-old observed relationship might no longer be needed. In its place, they propose that solar wind speed might be dependent on the distance from the coronal hole boundary. Eos also reports that this approach showed better agreement between observations and models than with the original relationship alone.
- **Context:** The debate predates this paper. A later study notes that the practical importance of the inverse relationship between observed solar wind speed and expansion factor is without dispute, while the physical interpretation and relevance behind it has been debated ever since.

A critical scientiﬁc goal in the space weather research and prediction community is to develop, implement and optimize numerical models for specifying the large-scale properties of solar wind conditions at the inner boundary of the heliospheric model domain. Here we present an adaptive prediction system that fuses information from in situ measurements of the solar wind into numerical models to better match the global solar wind model solutions near the Sun with prevailing physical conditions in the vicinity of Earth. In this way, we attempt to advance the predictive capabilities of well-established solar wind models for specifying solar wind speed, including the Wang-Sheeley-Arge (WSA) model. In particular, we use the Heliospheric Upwind eXtrapolation (HUX) model for mapping the solar wind solutions from the near-Sun environment to the vicinity of Earth. In addition, we present the newly developed Tunable HUX (THUX) model which solves the viscous form of the underlying Burgers equation. We perform a statistical analysis of the resulting solar wind predictions for the time 2006–2015. The proposed prediction scheme improves all the investigated coronal/heliospheric model combinations and produces better estimates of the solar wind state at Earth than our reference baseline model. We discuss why this is the case, and conclude that our ﬁndings have important implications for future practice in applied space weather research and prediction. The paper is Jian et al. (2011), *Solar Physics* vol. 273, issue 1, pp. 179–203, DOI 10.1007/s11207-011-9858-7. The search confirmed the bibliographic details and the abstract, though I did not access the full text.

- **Authors and publication:** The CU Experts record lists nine authors: Jian, Russell, Luhmann, MacNeice, Odstrcil, Riley, Linker, Skoug, and Steinberg. It gives an October 1, 2011 publication date and the pages above. The record marks the paper's access as closed.
- **Scope:** The study covers the 2004 latitudinal alignment of ACE and Ulysses. ACE and Ulysses encountered two stream interaction regions each Carrington rotation from 2016 to 2018, at 1 and 5.4 AU, respectively.
- **Key findings:** More SIR-driven shocks were observed at 5.4 AU than at 1 AU. Three small SIRs at 1 AU merged to form a strong SIR at 5.4 AU.
- **Model comparison:** The authors compared Enlil results on four points: the newer WSA v2.2 and Enlil v2.7 against older versions, sensitivity to magnetogram source (MWO vs. NSO), sensitivity to coronal model (WSA vs. MAS), and predictive capability at 1 AU versus 5.4 AU. The models capture field sector boundaries with some time offset. Although the new versions improved SIR timing prediction, the offset can be up to two days at 1 AU and four days at 5.4 AU.

- **What the paper found:** Using 14 magnetic maps from five observatory types around 2010 July, the authors compared MHD and potential-field source-surface models. Models with coronal hole areas close to EUV observations produced too little interplanetary flux. Matching the interplanetary flux required open regions larger than the observed holes. [Source: reading-clone.eprints-hosting.org/73134]
- **Flux-based check:** Estimating open flux directly from observed coronal holes plus synoptic maps also came out low, so the authors suggested either the observatory maps underestimate the Sun's flux or much of the open flux comes from regions not dark in EUV or X-rays. - **Follow-up:** A 2023 BAAS synopsis by Linker and co-authors argues the deficit is an observed problem rather than only a model problem, and that resolving it needs high-latitude line-of-sight magnetograms. [Source: baas.aas.org/pub/2023n3i240/download/pdf]
